passages.t: The workers in the vineyard: hired through the day
passages.happening:
Jesus tells a story. The kingdom of heaven is like a landowner who goes out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard. He agrees to pay them a denarius for the day and sends them in.

About the third hour he goes out again and sees others standing in the marketplace doing nothing. “You also go into my vineyard,” he tells them, and he will pay them whatever is right. He does the same at the sixth hour and the ninth.

About the eleventh hour he finds still others standing around. “Why have you been standing here all day long doing nothing?” he asks. “Because no one has hired us,” they answer. So he sends them into his vineyard too.

This story is found only in Matthew.
passages.hearers:
The story answers Peter's question at the end of the last chapter: “What then will there be for us?” (19:27). It is framed by the same saying at both ends: the last will be first, and the first last (19:30; 20:16).

Day labourers gathered in the village marketplace at dawn and waited to be hired. They were paid by the day and lived on each day's pay. At harvest, when grapes had to be picked and pressed before they spoiled, a vineyard owner might need many hands.

A denarius was a silver coin, the usual pay for a day's work in the fields. Roman soldiers of the time earned less. The historian Tacitus tells how, in AD 14, soldiers paid ten small copper coins a day mutinied and demanded a denarius a day (Annals 1.17). So a denarius was a fair day's wage.

The hours are counted from sunrise, about six in the morning. The third hour is about nine, the sixth about noon, the ninth about three in the afternoon, and the eleventh about five, one hour before the day's work ended.

Who would still be standing in the market at five o'clock? The ones no one wanted: the old, the weak, the slow. ‘No one has hired us’ was a hard thing to say. A day without work could mean a family without bread that night. Notice that the owner does not blame them. He sends them in.
passages.ot:
Israel was often pictured as God's vineyard. Isaiah sang, “For the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are the plant of His delight” (Isaiah 5:7). A hearer would catch at once that the owner of the vineyard stands for God.

The Law protected the hired worker: “You are to pay his wages each day before sunset, because he is poor and depends on them” (Deuteronomy 24:15).
passages.asks: The owner kept going back to the marketplace, all day long, looking for people to bring in. Ask whom you have written off as too late, or not worth hiring. And if you feel you came to God late, or have stood all day with no one choosing you, hear his question and his answer: ‘You also go into my vineyard.’

passages.t: Paid the same: are you envious because I am generous?
passages.happening:
When evening comes, the owner tells his foreman to call the workers and pay them, starting with the last ones hired. Those hired at the eleventh hour each receive a denarius. When the first workers come, they expect more. But each of them also receives a denarius.

They grumble against the landowner. “These men who were hired last worked only one hour,” they say, “and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden and the scorching heat of the day” (verse 12).

He answers one of them: ‘Friend, I am not being unfair to you. Did you not agree with me on one denarius? Take your pay and go. I want to give this last man the same as I gave you. Do I not have the right to do as I please with what is mine? Or are you envious because I am generous?’ (verses 13-15). “So the last will be first, and the first will be last” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The owner pays the last first, so that the first workers watch what the latecomers get. The hearer, like the first workers, waits for a sliding scale. It never comes.

‘Friend’ is a polite word with an edge. Matthew uses it only three times, each time to someone in the wrong: here, to the guest without wedding clothes (22:12), and to Judas in the garden (26:50).

The owner's last question uses an old idiom. In Greek it is, literally, ‘Is your eye evil because I am good?’ The BSB renders it ‘are you envious because I am generous?’ In the ancient world an ‘evil eye’ meant envy and grudging, the sour look at someone else's good fortune. A ‘good eye’ meant a generous one. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, tells that when Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai asked his students for the good way a person should hold to, Rabbi Eliezer answered, ‘a good eye’ (Avot 2:9). The workers hired at dawn received exactly what they agreed to, yet the landowner's goodness to the latecomers feels to them like a loss of their own. In a world that thought good things were limited, that was the natural reaction. The parable asks the hearer to see generosity without counting it as theft.

There is a later Jewish parable that makes a good comparison. The Jerusalem Talmud, put together several centuries after Jesus, tells of a king who paid a worker hired late a full day's wage, because he had done more in two hours than the others did all day (Berakhot 2:8). In that story the late worker earns it. In Jesus' story the latecomers earn nothing extra. They are paid because the owner is good.
passages.ot:
The Law used the same picture of the eye. It warned Israel not to “look upon your poor brother begrudgingly and give him nothing” when the year of release drew near (Deuteronomy 15:9). The Hebrew there is, literally, to let your eye be evil toward him.

The grumbling recalls Jonah, who was angry that God spared Nineveh: “I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God” (Jonah 4:2). Jonah's complaint was not that God was unjust. It was that God was kind to the wrong people.
passages.hard:
Isn't the owner unfair to those who worked all day? That is how it feels, and it is meant to. But notice what the owner says. No one was cheated. The first workers got what they agreed to, a fair day's wage, paid on time as the Law required. Their complaint is that others were treated generously.

Readers have taken the story in several ways. Many hear in it Jesus' defence of his welcome to tax collectors and sinners, who came late to God and were received in full, while some who had kept the Law all their lives resented it. Read where Matthew sets it, after Peter's ‘What then will there be for us?’, it warns disciples not to think of the kingdom as a wage system in which those who give up more deserve more. Others hear in it the welcome of non-Jews alongside Jewish believers. Gregory the Great, a bishop of Rome, preaching in 591, read the hours as the ages of the world and also as the stages of a single life, from childhood to old age, so that no one should despair of being called late. These readings can stand together.

Some modern readers do not take the owner as a picture of God at all. The New Testament scholar Amy-Jill Levine, in her book Short Stories by Jesus, reads him as a vineyard owner who hires everyone who needs work and pays each of them enough to live: a challenge to how people with money treat those who work for them. Others have read him far more darkly, as a rich man who shames a worker for speaking up. These notes do not choose among the readings.

One thing the story does not do is excuse unfair pay. The owner pays everyone at least a full day's wage, on the day it is earned. Nothing here lets an employer pay workers less than is right.
passages.asks: Which worker are you? If you came early and have served long, ask whether you can rejoice when grace goes to someone who came late. If you came late, hear that the gift was never wages. And ask where your eye has turned sour at someone else's good.

passages.t: Going up to Jerusalem: the third warning
passages.happening: As Jesus is going up to Jerusalem, he takes the twelve disciples aside. “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes” (verse 18). They will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified. “And on the third day He will be raised to life” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
This is the third of Jesus' warnings about his death (16:21; 17:22-23), and the fullest. It is the only one in Matthew that names crucifixion. Mark's version says ‘kill’. Matthew says ‘crucified’.

The ‘Gentiles’ means non-Jews. Here it points to the Romans, who ruled Judea. Crucifixion was a Roman punishment. Each step Jesus names will come to pass in Matthew's last chapters: handed over (26:47-50), judged by the council to deserve death (26:66), handed to Pilate (27:2), mocked (27:29), flogged and crucified (27:26).

People always spoke of going ‘up’ to Jerusalem. The city stands high in the hills. The note on Mark 10 tells how steep the road from Jericho was. Jesus walks it knowing all of this.
passages.ot: Isaiah's servant was treated in the same way: “I offered My back to those who struck Me, and My cheeks to those who tore out My beard. I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle” (Isaiah 50:6). And the hope of being raised on the third day echoes Hosea: “on the third day He will raise us up” (Hosea 6:2).
passages.asks: Jesus told them the whole road ahead, every hard step, and walked it anyway. Ask where you are tempted to follow Jesus only as far as the road is easy, and what it would mean to trust him with the steps you can already see coming.

passages.t: The mother of James and John: not to be served, but to serve
passages.happening:
The mother of Zebedee's sons comes to Jesus with her sons and kneels to ask a favour. “What do you want?” he asks. “Declare that in Your kingdom one of these two sons of mine may sit at Your right hand, and the other at Your left” (verse 21).

“You do not know what you are asking,” Jesus says to them. “Can you drink the cup I am going to drink?” “We can,” the brothers answer. Jesus tells them they will indeed drink his cup, but the seats at his right and left are not his to grant. They belong to those for whom his Father has prepared them.

The other ten hear about it and are indignant with the two brothers. Jesus calls them together. The rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them. “It shall not be this way among you” (verse 26). Whoever wants to be great must be a servant, and whoever wants to be first must be a slave, “just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many” (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this scene too (Mark 10:35-45), and the note on Mark 10 explains the cup, the seats and the ransom. In Mark, James and John ask for themselves. In Matthew, their mother asks. But Jesus answers the sons: ‘You do not know what you are asking.’ And it is the brothers who say, ‘We can.’ The request was theirs too.

She comes kneeling, the way a person came before a king to ask a favour. To sit at a king's right and left meant the highest places of honour and power. She has heard her sons' teacher speak of a kingdom, and she wants the best for them. Many parents would understand her.

Matthew alone tells where she will be later. At the cross, among the women watching from a distance, is “the mother of Zebedee’s sons” (27:56). And Matthew tells who is at Jesus' right and left when he is lifted up under the sign ‘King of the Jews’: “Two robbers were crucified with Him, one on His right hand and the other on His left” (27:38). She asked for her sons to have the places at his side in glory. She will see what those places looked like.

Jesus' word that they would drink his cup came true. James was the first of the Twelve to die for his faith: Herod “had James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword” (Acts 12:2).

A ‘ransom’ was the price paid to set someone free: a slave, a prisoner of war, or a person whose life was forfeit under the law (Exodus 21:30).
passages.ot:
The title Son of Man comes from Daniel 7. There one like a son of man is given a kingdom, and “the people of every nation and language should serve Him” (Daniel 7:14). Jesus turns the picture over. This Son of Man came to serve.

The prophets spoke of “the cup of His fury” (Isaiah 51:17), and a psalm says “a cup is in the hand of the LORD” (Psalm 75:8). In Isaiah 53, God's servant suffers for others, and “He bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:12). Many readers hear that chapter behind ‘a ransom for many’.
passages.hard:
What does it mean that Jesus' life was ‘a ransom for many’, and who was paid? Christians have answered in several ways. Some early Christian writers spoke of a ransom paid to the devil, who held people captive. Others rejected that idea. Many later teachers, including the Reformers, taught that Jesus' death meets the demands of God's justice, with God himself paying in the Son. Others stress that the cross is a victory that frees captives from sin and death. Many hold that ‘ransom’ is a picture of cost and freedom, not a deal with someone who must be named. Scholars also debate how directly the saying draws on Isaiah 53, since Isaiah does not use the word ransom.

All Christians agree on what Matthew puts first. The one who could have been served chose to serve, and he gave his own life so that many would go free.

A word of care. ‘Whoever wants to be great must be your servant’ has sometimes been turned against people, to keep them under someone who misuses power over them. Jesus says the opposite. He forbids his followers to ‘lord it over’ anyone. Serving others is never a duty to stay under mistreatment. If someone in your home or church is using power to harm you, telling someone you trust and seeking safety is not a failure to serve.
passages.asks: The mother asked for thrones, and the ten were angry because they wanted the same. Ask where you want the honour of following Jesus without the cost, for yourself or for those you love. Then ask a plainer question. Where could you serve this week in a way no one will notice or thank you for? That is greatness, Jesus says.

passages.happening:
As they leave Jericho, a large crowd follows Jesus. Two blind men are sitting beside the road. When they hear that Jesus is passing by, they cry out, “Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!” (verse 30). The crowd tells them to be quiet, but they cry out all the louder.

Jesus stops and calls them. “What do You want Me to do for you?” he asks. “Lord,” they answer, “let our eyes be opened.” Moved with compassion, Jesus touches their eyes. At once they receive their sight, and they follow him.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this story of one man, Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46-52), and the note on Mark 10 explains Jericho, the pilgrim road, and the title ‘Son of David’. Matthew tells it more briefly, without the name or the cloak. He adds two things of his own. Jesus is ‘moved with compassion’, and he touches their eyes.

Notice the question. Jesus asks the blind men exactly what he asked the mother of James and John a few verses earlier: ‘What do you want?’ She asked for seats of power. They ask to see. Matthew sets the two answers side by side. And the chapter's last words are that they followed him, on the road that leads to Jerusalem and the cross.
passages.ot: Isaiah promised a day when “the eyes of the blind will be opened” (Isaiah 35:5). ‘Son of David’ named the king God promised to David, a son whose throne would last forever (2 Samuel 7:13). Jesus is about to enter David's city.
passages.hard:
Mark and Luke tell of one blind man. Matthew tells of two. And Luke says it happened as Jesus came near Jericho (Luke 18:35), while Mark and Matthew say as he was leaving. How do these fit?

Readers have answered in several ways. Augustine argued that there were two men, and that Mark names only the one who was better known; to tell of one is not to deny the other. Many scholars think doubling is part of how Matthew tells stories: he also has two men troubled by demons where Mark has one (8:28), and he tells of two blind men earlier (9:27-31). Some suggest Matthew wanted two witnesses, as the Law required (Deuteronomy 19:15). On the place, some note that there were two Jerichos in Jesus' day, the old ruined city and the newer town Herod had built near it, so that a person could be leaving one while coming near the other. Others hold that ancient writers, like good storytellers, shortened and arranged details without being thought false.

Christians who hold a high view of Scripture are found on more than one side here. These notes do not choose. What all three Gospels agree on is the heart of it: on the road near Jericho, blind men cried to the Son of David for mercy, received their sight, and followed him.
passages.asks: If Jesus stopped and asked you, ‘What do you want Me to do for you?’, what would you say? The mother of James and John asked for a high place. The blind men asked to see. Ask which prayer is closer to yours. Then notice what they did with their sight. They followed him.
